title: Grace mostly means God's favour, sometimes his created gifts
source_text: THESIS I. JUXTA communem Doctorum Scholae Reformatae sensum Gratia ut plurimum designat ipsum Dei amorem & favorem quo nos immerentes prosequitur, aliquando vero etiam quaedam ejus dona & effecta creata. Sic Tilenus thesibus de variis divinae voluntatis nominibus disputatione prima thesi 20. docet Dei gratiam sumi active & passive. Ac prior, inquit, significatio benignam & propensam Dei voluntatem omnia liberaliter & gratis, non ex merito nostro, vel ex debito, imo largientem. Posterior donum aliquod gratis datum declarat.
pass_a_gloss: THESIS I. According to the common sense of the Doctors of the Reformed School Grace for the most part designates the very love and favour of God by which he follows us undeserving, but sometimes also certain gifts and created effects of it. So Tilenus in the theses on the various names of the divine will, first disputation thesis 20, teaches that the grace of God is taken actively and passively. And the former, he says, signification declares the kind and inclined will of God bestowing all things liberally and freely, not from our merit, or from debt, nay. The latter declares some gift freely given.
pass_b_english: Thesis I. In the common understanding of the doctors of the Reformed school, grace usually means God's own love and favour, with which he pursues us though we do not deserve it. Sometimes, though, it also means certain created gifts and effects of that favour.

So Tilenus, in the first disputation of his theses on the various names of the divine will (thesis 20), teaches that God's grace is taken both actively and passively. In the first sense, he says, it means God's kind and well-disposed will, which, far from acting out of our merit or as a debt, rather bestows everything generously and freely. In the second it means some gift given freely.

choices.why: Tilenus's terms: grace as God's own favour (active) and grace as a gift received (passive).
